Plug an interpreter into Run.what: Another extension's debugger can be the one Run starts; its worker reads and writes the workspace through the editor, under the same policy as any run.

Starter interpreter.what: A template extension you can fork, whose interpreter runs a file when you press Run, and which is rebuilt and reloaded into the editor as you change it.

Starter code renderer.what: The template's Reopen Editor With → Rendered view: a custom editor that shows a file rendered and writes your changes back to its text.

Extensions by URL.what: Load extensions from outside the editor (an interpreter or renderer from editor-contrib) by URL, reloading as they're rebuilt.

Architecture reports and metrics.what: Every context reports itself and its traffic on the architecture plane, and its memory, timing and traffic numbers on the metrics plane, for debug-mcp (architecture_state, metrics_query) and the architecture harness.

Sign in with GitHub.what: Signs a person in to the editor or the admin app with their GitHub account, through a GitHub App that reads only their numeric GitHub id.
Sign in with GitHub.docs: packages/api/README.md, *A GitHub App, not an OAuth App*

Sign in by email code.what: Signs a person in with a one-time code emailed to their address, which they type in or reach through the email's link.

Sign in with a password, and reset it.what: Lets a person set a password, sign in with their email and password, and reset a forgotten password using a code sent by email.

Two-factor sign-in.what: Adds a second step to sign-in: a code from an authenticator app or an emailed code, plus recovery codes for getting back in.

Sign in with a passkey.what: Lets a person register passkeys, sign in with one instead of a password, and remove them.

Link sign-in methods and merge accounts.what: Lets a person add a GitHub account or another email address to their account, and merge in a separate account that already had it.

Hosted sign-in and DPoP tokens for clien.what: Gives every client app one locked-down sign-in page on the API (started by a pushed authorization request), so no app's own page ever sees a password; the app then gets short-lived DPoP-bound access tokens and rotating refresh tokens, plus OAuth metadata and a JWKS.

Manage your sign-ins and delete your acc.what: Lets a person see the sessions signed in as them, revoke one or all of them, and delete their account; deleted data is purged after a grace period.
Manage your sign-ins and delete your acc.docs: packages/api/README.md, *Identity and the data we keep*

Your account page.what: One Preact account page, shared by the editor and the admin app, for managing ways to sign in, passkeys, two-factor and a password.

GitHub API proxy.what: Passes the editor's GitHub API calls, a clone's git reads, a push, and CI's reads (a commit's runs, a run's jobs, a job's log) through to GitHub with the user's GitHub token kept on the server, and refuses anything else.

Admin: sign-in and roles.what: Gives the admin app its own sign-in, separate from the editor's, and shows each person only the pages their roles allow.

Admin: overview and users.what: Shows an overview page and the list of accounts, and for each user their identities, sessions and audit rows.

Admin: sign-ins and their timelines.what: Lists live sign-ins and lets an admin revoke one or open its timeline: the requests, editor events, audit rows and errors in order.

Admin: architecture.what: Shows the API as it describes itself: its routes, data stores and tables, the GitHub calls it passes through, who calls it, and what it calls.

Rate limits.what: Refuses sign-in, token and error-report requests that go over per-IP or per-target limits, before doing the work.

Unusual sign-ins.what: Scores each sign-in's requests and client against a learned model of normal behavior (without keeping the actual values), and lists the unusual ones, worst first, in the admin app.

Tamper-evident audit log.what: Records every security event (sign-ins, refusals, account changes) in D1 and in locked R2 copies that can't be changed or deleted, and shows the log in the admin app.

Kill switch and switches.what: Lets the owner pause the whole API (maintenance mode) or smaller parts of it from the admin app, and the health and status endpoints report it.
Kill switch and switches.docs: packages/api/README.md, *The kill switch (O1) and narrower switches (O8)*

Traffic and cost guard.what: Shows Cloudflare's traffic analytics (top paths, user agents, status codes) in the admin app, checks the account's spend every hour, and alerts or pauses if usage runs away.

Tripwire.what: Checks every row a signed-in request reads and treats any row that belongs to another user as an incident, alerting the owner.

Errors with quotable ids.what: Every uncaught error, the API's and the editor's alike, gets an id the person is shown to quote; errors are grouped, and the admin app shows each occurrence with a source-mapped stack and, for a signed-in session, what happened just before.

Email, inbox and the Mail page.what: Sends the API's email, receives mail for its own addresses, runs a full email sign-in smoke test, sends alerts to the owner, and shows all of this on the admin app's Mail page.

Redacted logging.what: Sends all of the API's logs and traces through one allowlist, so nothing personal or secret is ever logged.

Sites on unusuallygood.dev.what: Serves the root domain (which redirects browsers to the editor and asks anything else to pay over x402), the editor and the admin app as Cloudflare sites; only the root domain runs a Worker.

debug-mcp server.what: Runs a local collector that the editor's hubs connect to over a WebSocket, and offers what they send to an agent as MCP tools over stdio.

Query logs and spans.what: Lets an agent query the live editor's log records and timed spans from all its contexts, or wait until a matching record arrives.

Metrics.what: Samples gauges in every context once a second (memory, frame rate, long frames, durations, data channels) and lets an agent query them.

Live architecture and payload capture.what: Reports every context (hubs, workers, extension hosts, webviews, network endpoints) and the traffic between them, with optional capture of message payloads, for an agent and for the editor's architecture view.

Connected tabs and hub tree health.what: Finds the editor tabs and preview apps connected right now (flagging ones on an outdated protocol) so tools can target one, and gives a health snapshot of the hub tree.

Page tools.what: Lets a page offer its own tools, such as evaluating JavaScript or running a CSS selector in the live page, which debug-mcp passes to an agent for one tab.

Observe an app (opt-in debug link).what: One call that sends an app's logs, console output and errors onto its hub, keeps a preview app's records under their own scope, and connects to debug-mcp on localhost or when ?debug is set.

Composable message hubs.what: A message bus for each window, frame or worker, linked into a tree with permissions on each link, so a message crosses a boundary only when something on the other side wants it; it comes with a simulated network for deterministic tests.

Hub request/reply.what: Lets one context serve a named request and another context call it across the hub tree, with timeouts and an error when nobody answers.

Hub links over WebRTC, and tab lobbies.what: Links hubs in two pages over a WebRTC data channel, and groups a browser's open tabs into a lobby with one tab chosen as host.

silo features.what: Lists every way into a program (commands, views, settings, buttons, agent tools, hub requests and more) by reading its code.
silo features.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *Derived history: features, reach, what runs say (built 2026-10-12; the feature layer parked)*

silo history.what: Tells what changed in a program from snapshots of its code along git's first-parent history, never from commit messages.
silo history.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *Derived history: features, reach, what runs say (built 2026-10-12; the feature layer parked)*

silo check.what: Reports where the feature ledger or this manifest and the code disagree (a stopped feature still in the code, a removed one still documented, a way in no feature owns) and fails CI on it.
silo check.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *The feature ledger: code keeps its place, or goes (designed 2026-10-12; step 1 built 2026-10-23)*

silo status.what: Records a decision about a feature (active, experimental, stopped and so on) in the shared feature ledger.
silo status.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *The feature ledger: code keeps its place, or goes (designed 2026-10-12; step 1 built 2026-10-23)*

silo remove and restore.what: Takes a feature out of the code (the files only it uses, plus its manifest entries) and leaves a tombstone that can bring it back later.
silo remove and restore.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *The feature ledger: code keeps its place, or goes (designed 2026-10-12; step 1 built 2026-10-23)*

silo coverage.what: Shows what the runs saved in .silo/ executed, commit by commit: what started or stopped running, and what was never reached.
silo coverage.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *Which tests reach what (designed 2026-10-22; the record built 2026-10-23)*

silo init.what: Sets up .silo/ in a repository, with its git settings and a baseline of what the code imports.

silo install.what: Installs dependencies with the project's package manager, skipping anything published in the last week.

Run TypeScript in the interpreter.what: Runs TypeScript source straight from its syntax tree, synchronously or async, and returns the value of the last expression.

tsval step debugger.what: Steps through a run one step at a time, pauses and resumes it, sets breakpoints, and snapshots or forks the running state.

Host seams, modules and types.what: Lets a host inspect every value and call that crosses in from the host, watch statements and coverage, hook async calls, resolve imports (almostnode does this in the editor), and optionally add TypeScript's type checker.

Explore event-loop schedules.what: Runs a program under every distinct event-loop ordering to find all its possible outcomes and races, each with a schedule that replays it.

Conformance suites.what: Tests tsval against test262 and TypeScript's own test cases, with scripts to fetch, sample and report on them.

Parse TypeScript into a lossless CST.what: Our own BABLR grammar for the TypeScript subset tsval runs; it parses source into a syntax tree that keeps every character, as spans (sync or async), and has a command-line parser and a parse version for checking caches.

In-browser Node runtime (almostnode).what: Runs bundled Node programs, such as language servers, on the browser's main thread, with Node's built-in modules, an in-memory file system, and HTTP servers that a service worker routes requests to.
In-browser Node runtime (almostnode).docs: packages/almostnode/README.md, *Node's built-ins: unenv, Node's own code, and ours where we must differ*

Editor API: run contract for debuggers.what: What a debugger extension and its worker send and answer during a run: custom debug events (values, coverage, effects, ended, ask and others), requests (decide, stdin, getCoverage), a live-values recorder, recorded values for replay, the workspace's files as almostnode's VirtualFS, and the editor's network probes.

Editor API: annotations and pane views.what: Lets an extension attach things to a range of code so they stay with that code as the file changes, and add a tab beside every editor drawn from its own data.

Editor API: capability policy and gate.what: Lets an extension read the capability policy and a run's effects, get the gate's verdict, run untrusted code in a locked-down realm, and read or edit rules.

Editor API: what the editor keeps.what: Lets an extension read the runtime evidence kept for a file, CPU profiles, whether something is a service or a task, how a worker failed, and the editor's git status with BABLR's verdict on each change.

Web Awesome lint rules.what: ESLint rules that flag native HTML elements that have a Web Awesome equivalent, and HTML or CSS written inside strings.

Brand theme.what: Sets up Web Awesome with its design tokens adjusted for the brand, following the system's light or dark mode, with or without Web Awesome's native styles, and kept within a size budget.

Theme follows VS Code's color theme.what: Maps the theme onto whichever VS Code color theme is active in the workbench.

Web Awesome components through the theme.what: The only way for app code to load the Web Awesome components it is allowed to use.

Recipes, surface styles and Stitches.what: Gives each part of the app its own styles and the app's shared shapes as recipe classes, all written with Stitches in an ordered set of style layers.

Published theme components.what: Components published for use outside the app: the movable, collapsible <app-window> element (and an appWindow() function), plus caption, code, frame and toolbar recipes, each a class you get from a function call.

VS Code look for Web Awesome.what: A published Web Awesome theme in VS Code's default colors that follows the live color theme when used inside VS Code or a webview.
VS Code look for Web Awesome.docs: packages/theme/README.md, *The look: Web Awesome as VS Code*

Release pipeline.what: Each push to main tests, builds and publishes every package as a GitHub release tarball and deploys the site, with no npm registry.

Architecture suites and performance budg.what: Browser suites tour the real editor (runs, previews, capabilities, sessions), record what each test reached for CI's evidence, and hold boot time, hover latency, a large repo's load and memory to budgets.

Weekly ledger cleanup.what: Each week CI runs `silo check` and opens one pull request deleting the first dormant way in that `silo remove` can take out.
